title: The miracle of the Qur'an
hookLine: a challenge sits inside the book itself: bring one surah like it

lines: A BOOK THAT SETS A TEST.
THE CHALLENGE IS ON THE PAGE.
cards: A book usually asks to be believed. This one sets a test.

In the second surah, al-Baqarah, the Qur'an turns to anyone who doubts where it came from and says, in Pickthall's translation: "then produce a surah of the like thereof, and call your witness beside Allah if ye are truthful."
Not the whole book. One surah. The challenge is printed in the middle of the text it's defending, and it is read aloud whenever that surah is recited.

teach.b: The word is i'jaz. Lane's old Arabic lexicon puts it under a root about being unable, falling short. A mu'jizah, a miracle, is a sign that leaves others unable to match it.
Musa had his staff. 'Isa, in the Qur'an, healed the blind. So what was the sign given to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him?
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari gives his own answer, in paraphrase: every prophet was given signs that led people to believe, and what I was given is revelation that Allah revealed to me.
The miracle, Muslims say, is the book.

Another verse widens the challenge, Pickthall again: "though mankind and the jinn should assemble to produce the like of this Qur'an, they could not produce the like thereof though they were helpers one of another."

Then the theologians got to work, and they did not all agree on what exactly can't be matched. Al-Baqillani, who wrote a whole book on i'jaz, pointed to its eloquence, which he held was beyond the reach of Arabic poetry.
Al-Jurjani pointed to its nazm, the way its words are joined and arranged. Some pointed to what it tells of things unseen.
And one Mu'tazili thinker, al-Nazzam, is remembered for a different answer: people could have matched it, but Allah turned them away from trying.
Other scholars rejected that view, but it shows how seriously the question was taken.

teach.h: EACH PROPHET'S SIGN, AND THIS ONE A BOOK.
teach.b: So this part ends where it began, with kalam: faith asking questions of its own book.
A staff or a healing is seen once.

teach.h: A SIGN YOU CAN OPEN AGAIN.
teach.b: A book can be opened again tomorrow.

how: Muslims speak of the Qur'an as the Prophet's lasting miracle, and scholars of Arabic rhetoric and theology have written works on i'jaz, studying what in its language and arrangement they hold cannot be matched.

o: the art of beautiful Qur'an calligraphy on mosque walls
the teaching that the Qur'an's words can't be matched
the beauty of a skilled reciter's voice when reciting aloud

practice: Choose one verse you know: al-Fatiha's opening line, or al-Ikhlas, or, if you don't know any in Arabic, today's line from al-Baqarah in English.

Say it out loud, slowly, at a normal speaking voice, then a second time, slower, listening to the sounds as they leave you. Then sit in the quiet it leaves behind, and let the last word ring for a moment.

wordCard.voice: I'jaz. The inimitability of the Qur'an: the teaching that its words can't be matched, which Muslims hold as the Prophet's sign. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: inimitability, from a root about being unable or falling short.

carryVoice: Your line: the book as sign. A sign you can open again, any day you like. Tomorrow a new part begins.
